# Mercenaries, militias and the loyalty of armed men (`mercenaries_citizen_militia`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/military.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Warfare, security & deterrence (`military`)
- Deps: helped by standing_army_logistics, conscription_mass_army, banking_credit
- Core idea: Whoever pays and commands the soldiers holds the state. Hired captains (in Italy the condottieri, who served under a written contract, the condotta) are skilled but serve for pay: they prolong wars, change sides, and can seize power, as Francesco Sforza did in Milan in 1450. Citizen militias are loyal but, without training and experienced officers, are beaten by professionals. The lasting solution is a force raised from the ruler's own subjects, trained and paid by the state, with officers appointed and promoted by the state and not owning their units.
- Pitfalls:
  - Repeating Machiavelli's claim that condottieri fought bloodless sham battles; Mallett showed their wars were real and their skill high
  - Machiavelli's own militia ran at Prato in 1512; enthusiasm does not replace training
  - Late-paid mercenaries are more dangerous than the enemy
  - Late republican Rome shows the same problem with citizens: soldiers who expect land from their general follow him against the state
- History: greece: 401 BC – the Ten Thousand, Greek mercenaries in Persian service (Xenophon); africa: 241–238 BC – Carthage nearly destroyed by its own unpaid mercenaries; rome: 88 BC – Sulla marches on Rome; 49 BC – Caesar crosses the Rubicon with an army loyal to him personally; islamic: 9th c. – Abbasid slave soldiers (mamluks); 1250 – Mamluks take power in Egypt; china: 755 – An Lushan, frontier general of a professional army, rebels against the Tang; europe: 14th–15th c. – condottieri in Italy; 1506 – Machiavelli's Florentine militia; 1527 – unpaid imperial troops sack Rome; 1620s–1630s – Wallenstein, the greatest military contractor
- Read:
  - Niccolò Machiavelli, Il Principe, chapters 12–13 (written 1513, printed 1532)
  - Michael Mallett, Mercenaries and Their Masters: Warfare in Renaissance Italy (1974)
  - David Parrott, The Business of War (2012)
